prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: Having read all eight opening ballots, I move my preferred configuration from my own first choice (B043, Car-Parrinello) to B005. It is the only candidate that seven of eight members place in their top three, and the reasons given are scientific rather than merely popular. The magic-wavelength lattice clock combines Lamb-Dicke confinement with thousands of atoms and has reached roughly 1e-18 fractional uncertainty, confirmed by several independent laboratories and compared across fibre links. As a theorist I am struck by what Eva Lindroth stresses: the agreement between calculated magic wavelengths and blackbody and lattice shifts and the measured clock behaviour is quantitative, which is the kind of reproducibility I value. The invention is clean to attribute (Katori for the concept and the first strontium realization, Ye for the record accuracy and many-body control), the scope is distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and the pending redefinition of the second makes the timing good.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is a precision-measurement and instrument achievement, and some colleagues may read it as an incremental refinement of work already honoured in 2005 (Hall and Hansch) and 2012 (Wineland). The credit list also omits Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde and others who contributed decisively to individual milestones, and the two names do not capture the full priority chronology. Finally, atomic physics is outside my core expertise, so I am partly relying on Lindroth, Kroll and Danielsson for the judgement of whether the lattice step is large enough to stand beside the earlier prizes. If the committee prefers a condensed-matter discovery with a new quantum state at its centre, B014 is the natural alternative and B043 remains my own scientific favourite, although it faces the method-versus-discovery question and the 1998 chemistry prize on DFT.

responses.point: The lattice clock is atomic physics at its most elegant, with exceptional theory-experiment agreement, but she notes that the overlap with the Hall-Hansch comb and Wineland ion prizes may make some colleagues see it as incremental.
responses.response: I agree on the quantitative theory-experiment link and I find it persuasive. On the overlap, I would hold that the earlier prizes honoured the comb as a ruler and the control of single trapped ions, whereas the lattice clock is a different mechanism: a magic-wavelength trap that lets many neutral atoms be interrogated without motional or Stark shifts, which is what gives the stability gain. The Wineland comparison is the harder one, and I would like you to say whether the many-atom lattice step is a real conceptual advance over single-ion clocks or mainly a gain in averaging.

responses.point: He ranks KPZ first as a clean universal mechanism with exact solutions and Takeuchi-Sano experiments, and B014 second, while questioning whether B005 is a discovery in the Nobel sense or precision engineering.
responses.response: I respect the elegance of KPZ and the exact-solution programme, but only one member ranks it, and he himself concedes the experimental verification is fewer and noisier than the theory, and that Parisi's 2021 prize and the credit spread among Spohn, Corwin, Quastel and others complicate the configuration. On the discovery question, I would say the clock is a measurement that nature answers back to, with tests of constants and relativistic redshift, so it qualifies as discovery-enabling. I do share your view that B014 is the more exciting condensed-matter physics, and I would keep it as the leading alternative if B005 stalls.

responses.point: She ranks aberration-corrected electron optics first and B014 third, and warns that credit in B014 is concentrated in the group leader while Yuan Cao, Dean, Efetov, Young and hBN encapsulation work are not credited.
responses.response: I take the Cao and Dean credit concern seriously and it is the main reason I do not push B014 as my first choice, since a three-name cap cannot reflect the experimental community. On B051 I think the instrumentation case is strong for materials spectroscopy, which I use daily, but only you rank it and the STEM-corrector credit question (Krivanek, Dellby) is open, so I cannot yet argue it as a lead candidate. I would be glad to hear whether the credit among Rose, Haider and Urban can be settled more firmly.

responses.point: He ranks B015 first for ultracold atoms in optical lattices realizing Hubbard models, noting that the three-name cap forces a choice between Esslinger, Greiner, Bloch and Zoller.
responses.response: I share the physical appeal, since it is a controlled realization of Hubbard physics in my own field's language, and I ranked it fifth with Esslinger rather than Zoller as the third name, so we disagree on that seat. The unresolved allocation, the overlap with the 2001 and 2012 prizes and the fact that the promised payoff, such as d-wave superconductivity in the Hubbard model, has not materialized make me hesitate to put it first now. I would keep it as a strong alternative and would like to hear how you weigh Zoller's theory against Esslinger's fermionic Mott insulator.

responses.point: He ranks IceCube first, valuing detector development leading to discovery, and sees confirmed diffuse flux and source identifications as well-timed.
responses.response: This is a clear case of experiment opening a new window and I do not dismiss it, but astroparticle physics is far from my expertise and I defer to you and Ulf Danielsson on it. My qualification is that the individual source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) are still at moderate significance, and the credit within a collaboration of several hundred plus the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND precursors makes a three-name choice contestable. B005 is cleaner on attribution and maturity, though I concede that IceCube may be the more natural prize for the longer term.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the lattice step as a sufficient advance beyond the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the SI second before recognizing the lattice clock.
Whether a method such as Car-Parrinello (B043) can be judged a physical discovery of the kind the Nobel Prize in Physics usually recognizes, given the 1998 chemistry prize for DFT.
For B014, how to treat the missing credit for Yuan Cao and other experimental groups, and whether the superconducting pairing mechanism needs to be settled first.
I have not independently verified priority details or accuracy figures and rely on recollection and the colleagues' ballots.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B005 (Katori, Ye). I note only that I ranked B043 first and that Car-Parrinello-type methods are part of the computational toolchain in my own field, though I have no personal tie to Car or Parrinello in my profile. I have no recorded connection to the B014, B015 or B020 candidates either.
